overview: Both are selective and differential media for Gram-negative rods, but their indicator systems give strikingly different visual clues.
genZNote: Pink colonies versus a green metallic sheen — same lactose story, different tell.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A selective and differential agar containing bile salts (to inhibit Gram-positives) and lactose with a pH indicator.
aspects.valueB: A selective and differential agar containing eosin and methylene blue dyes, which also inhibit Gram-positive organisms and indicate lactose fermentation.

aspects.label: Selective Agent
aspects.valueA: Bile salts and crystal violet inhibit most Gram-positive bacteria.
aspects.valueB: Eosin Y and methylene blue dyes inhibit most Gram-positive bacteria.

aspects.label: Differential Indicator
aspects.valueA: Neutral red pH indicator turns lactose fermenters pink to red.
aspects.valueB: Dye complex gives strong lactose fermenters a green metallic sheen, and E. coli a characteristic dark colony with green sheen.

aspects.label: Classic Diagnostic Appearance
aspects.valueA: Pink colonies (e.g. E. coli, Klebsiella) vs colorless colonies (e.g. Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus).
aspects.valueB: Green metallic sheen strongly suggests E. coli; other lactose fermenters appear dark pink/purple without the sheen.

aspects.label: Typical Use
aspects.valueA: Routine primary plating for stool and urine cultures to screen for enteric pathogens.
aspects.valueB: Used similarly, often preferred when a rapid, visually distinctive E. coli identification is wanted.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Uses bile salts and neutral red; lactose fermenters turn pink.
aspects.valueB: Uses eosin-methylene blue dyes; strong fermenters like E. coli show a green metallic sheen.
